public_context: A fictional river district uses temporary boarding slips when storm conditions interrupt ordinary ferry service. A small administrative dossier describes issuing slips, priority queues and later checks against records. The district, offices, people and scheme are invented. Discuss this particular arrangement rather than the law or practice of any real jurisdiction.

sources.source_text:
A memorandum signed by Mira Fenn in October 2013 describes the storm-boarding slip scheme in Mallow Ford. The West Quay Office issues temporary paper slips when the district marks ordinary ferry departures as disrupted by river conditions. The scheme concerns queue priority during a declared disruption, rather than ownership of a boat or a permanent ferry reservation.

The illustrated register contains 18 households distributed across three landing routes, with 6 listed on each route. A slip records the household identifier, landing route and issue day. The clerk stamps it with a square mark when issued; the later boarding steward uses a round mark after admitting the household. These two marks record different actions and must not be read as interchangeable evidence.

A household may join the priority queue at its listed landing on the issue day. If no departure occurs before that evening, the clerk can carry the same slip forward once by writing the next day beneath the original date. This extension requires confirmation that the route was still disrupted; it is not an automatic renewal for everyone holding a slip.

The memorandum describes a later check of 12 slips against the steward sheets. Of these, 10 have corresponding round boarding marks and 2 lack a matching steward entry. The author does not infer that the unmatched households deliberately avoided boarding: missing sheets and unused slips are both left possible. A clerk stamp alone therefore does not establish that a journey occurred.

One example concerns a household arriving at a different landing from the route printed on its slip. Staff direct it to the ordinary queue at that landing rather than alter the recorded route. The memorandum offers this as an application of the route rule. It does not establish a general policy for every emergency that might prevent a household reaching its assigned landing.

The scheme grants no separate priority for cargo. An absent boarding mark is not itself treated as an offence. No later review of lost-slip replacement was conducted.
